claim_verdicts.evidence: "ClusterRole, by contrast, is a non-namespaced resource." ... "Because ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped, you can also use them to grant access to: cluster-scoped resources (like nodes)" ... "This kind of reference lets you define a set of common roles across your cluster, then reuse them within multiple namespaces."

"A RoleBinding grants permissions within a specific namespace whereas a ClusterRoleBinding grants that access cluster-wide." "If you want to bind a ClusterRole to all the namespaces in your cluster, you use a ClusterRoleBinding." Authorization evaluates each request's attributes at request time (authorization.md: "The API server evaluates all of the request attributes against all policies"), so later namespaces are covered.

"A RoleBinding can also reference a ClusterRole to grant the permissions defined in that ClusterRole to resources inside the RoleBinding's namespace." Execution: outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/cluster-roles.txt shows `list pods -n donhang` yes, `list pods -n kube-system` no for junior-dev.

Round 2: claim and lesson narrowed to nodes ("a RoleBinding cannot grant nodes, whatever its ClusterRole lists"). rbac.md: "Because ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped, you can also use them to grant access to: cluster-scoped resources (like nodes)". Capture cluster-roles.txt: `can-i list nodes --as=junior-dev` -> warning 'not namespace scoped', then `no`. Claim text keeps the Namespace-object exception.

view: "Allows read-only access to see most objects in a namespace. It does not allow viewing roles or role bindings. This role does not allow viewing Secrets, since reading the contents of Secrets enables access to ServiceAccount credentials in the namespace, which would allow API access as any ServiceAccount in the namespace (a form of privilege escalation)."
cluster-admin: "Allows super-user access to perform any action on any resource."

"API servers create a set of default ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects." "At each start-up, the API server updates default cluster roles with any missing permissions" "Auto-reconciliation is enabled by default if the RBAC authorizer is active." User-facing roles include cluster-admin and view.

deploy/argocd/install.yaml (image quay.io/argoproj/argocd:v3.1.16): ClusterRole argocd-application-controller rules `apiGroups ['*'] resources ['*'] verbs ['*']` and `nonResourceURLs ['*'] verbs ['*']`; ClusterRoleBinding argocd-application-controller roleRef ClusterRole argocd-application-controller, subject ServiceAccount argocd-application-controller namespace argocd. Capture cluster-roles.txt lines 18-23 match.

Architecture page (WebFetch summary): "The application controller is a Kubernetes controller which continuously monitors running applications" ... "compares the current, live state against the desired target state (as specified in the repo)" ... "optionally takes corrective action." install.yaml StatefulSet argocd-application-controller has `serviceAccountName: argocd-application-controller`.

"Kubernetes reviews only the following API request attributes: user - The `user` string provided during authentication. group ... extra ..." followed by API, verb, resource, namespace etc.; no attribute carries a Git commit author.

Projects page (WebFetch summary): default project "permits deployments from any source repo, to any cluster, and all resource Kinds"; initial spec `sourceRepos: ['*']`, `destinations: namespace '*' server '*'`, `clusterResourceWhitelist: group '*' kind '*'`. Repo: apps/staging.yaml, policies-staging.yaml, edge-staging.yaml, traefik.yaml all `project: default`.

Round 2: opinion now conditioned in summary line 5 ("With Argo CD installed as on staging, config repository write access is as powerful as `cluster-admin`") and in the claim text; supported by claims 8 (controller bound to '*' cluster-wide) and 11 (project default allows all kinds).
